\chapter{La impresora de la sala 2}
\label{ch:es-oficina}
\hlchaptermodality{469}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can deal with a workplace machine that is not working: read a notice saying a printer is out of service, say what I want to print and what I cannot connect, and offer to make or return a phone call.}

Read a notice taped to a printer and a message from a colleague, then say what you will do.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[imprimir]{imprimir — to print}

\label{lesson:ES-C469-imprimir}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{el impreso} and \textbf{la prisa}. The first is this verb's participle and the second is its distant cousin.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: imprimir}
\textbf{imprimir} — to print.

\begin{quote}
Voy a \textbf{imprimir} el documento.
\end{quote}

\emph{Imprimir a doble cara} — to print on both sides, where \emph{cara} is the face of the sheet: the same word you learned for a face, lent to paper.

You already have the participle. When you learned \textbf{el impreso}, it was given to you as \emph{the irregular past participle of imprimir} — so the verb has been named in this book once, without ever being yours to use. Now it is.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the participle you already hold}]
Most Spanish verbs build a participle by rule. This one does not, and you have had the exception longer than the verb.

The irregular participles gave you \emph{hecho}, \emph{dicho}, \emph{visto} and \emph{puesto}; \emph{cubierto} and \emph{roto} joined the list later. \textbf{Impreso} belongs on it too.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{verb} & \textbf{participle} \\
\midrule
imprimir & \textbf{impreso} \\
escribir & escrito \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{He impreso el documento} — I have printed the document. You will also meet \emph{imprimido}, which the Academy allows, but \emph{impreso} is what a notice prints and what a printer's menu says.

And \emph{el impreso} as a \textbf{noun} — a form to fill in — is that same participle hardened, which is the move \emph{el pedido} taught you.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{imprimere}: \textbf{in-}, into, plus \textbf{premere}, to \textbf{press}. To print is to \textbf{press something into} a surface, which is exactly what a press does and exactly what the word has always meant.

\emph{Premere} is the root under \emph{la prisa} — a hurry is a pressing. Follow it outward and English fills up: \textbf{press}, \textbf{pressure}, \textbf{print}, \textbf{imprint}, \textbf{express} (pressed out), \textbf{compress}, \textbf{impression} — a mark pressed in, whether into wax or into a person.

So a printer does not \textquotedblleft{}produce\textquotedblright{} a page. Historically it \textbf{presses} one, and the word kept the machine in it long after the machine changed.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item I am going to print the document
  \item I have printed the document
  \item what premere means
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To print? (\textbf{Imprimir}.) Its participle? (\textbf{Impreso}.) What does \emph{premere} mean? (\textbf{To press}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la impresora]{la impresora — the printer}

\label{lesson:ES-C469-impresora}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{la lavadora} and \textbf{el impreso}. One lends the ending, the other lends the stem, and together they make the machine.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la impresora}
\textbf{la impresora} — the printer.

\begin{quote}
La \textbf{impresora} de la sala 2 está fuera de servicio.
\end{quote}

\emph{Una impresora en color} — a colour printer.

You could have reached this word before being told, which is what la lavadora promised: a machine is often its verb plus \textbf{-dora}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the article says which one you mean}]
El contador settled one thing already: the ending does not decide the article, since \emph{la lavadora} is feminine and \emph{el contador} masculine off the same \textbf{-dor}. Treat that as known.

What this word adds is a case where the article is not merely a fact to memorise but is \textbf{carrying the meaning}. \emph{Lavar} has no human washer in ordinary speech, so \textbf{-dora} was free to mean the machine and nothing else. \emph{Imprimir} is not like that. Printing was a trade long before it was a box on a desk, and the stem kept both.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Spanish} & \textbf{what it is} \\
\midrule
el impresor & the person who prints \\
la impresora & the machine that prints \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Say \emph{el impresor} about the box and you have promoted it to a tradesman. With \emph{contador} and \emph{lavadora} the article was something to learn; here it is something to choose.

English will not help you: it calls both of them a \textbf{printer} and leaves the sentence to sort it out. Spanish has decided in advance, in one letter.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Same \emph{imprimere} as the verb: \emph{in-} plus \emph{premere}, to press into.

Why feminine rather than masculine? \emph{El contador} told you the ending does not decide; this is the mechanism underneath. \emph{Impresora} started life as an adjective leaning on a noun — \emph{la máquina impresora}, the printing machine. The noun dropped away and left its gender behind. So the article you cannot predict from the ending was fixed by a word that is no longer said.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the printer in room 2 is out of service
  \item which one is the person and which is the machine
  \item the verb this machine was built from
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The printer? (\textbf{La impresora}.) Why feminine? (\textbf{Because \emph{la máquina} is} — the noun fell away and left its gender.) And the person? (\textbf{El impresor}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[conectar]{conectar — to connect}

\label{lesson:ES-C469-conectar}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{el ordenador}, then \textbf{imprimir}. Nothing gets printed until one more verb has happened.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: conectar}
\textbf{conectar} — to connect, to join one thing to another.

\begin{quote}
No puedo \textbf{conectar} la impresora al ordenador.
\end{quote}

The noun is \textbf{la conexión}, and it is worth a second look: the verb has a \textbf{c}, the noun has an \textbf{x}. Say \emph{co-ne-XIÓN}, weight on the last syllable.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: conectar and conectarse}]
The same verb does two different jobs depending on whether the thing being joined is an object out in front of you or yourself.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{what you mean} & \textbf{what you say} \\
\midrule
join a thing to something & \textbf{conectar} la impresora \\
get yourself online & \textbf{conectarse} a internet \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

So \emph{no me puedo conectar} means \emph{I can't get connected} — you, not the printer. The pronoun is doing the whole of that work, and dropping it turns the sentence into a report about some object you never named.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
The Academy's dictionary derives \textbf{conectar} from English \textbf{to connect} — and English had built that out of Latin \textbf{conectere}: \textbf{con-}, together, plus \textbf{nectere}, to \textbf{tie}.

So the Latin is real, and the route is not the one it looks like. The word did not sit in Spanish since Rome waiting for wires. It came in from English in the modern era, carrying Latin parts back to a Latin language.

You have now met that happening three ways in a row:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{el ordenador} — an old Spanish word that borrowed a new \emph{meaning} from French;
  \item \textbf{internet} — an English word borrowed whole, with only the beat changed;
  \item \textbf{conectar} — an English word borrowed as a shape, its pieces Latin all along.
\end{itemize}

\emph{Nectere} is a knot-word. English keeps it in \textbf{nexus}, a tying-together, and in \textbf{annex}, tied on. A \emph{nexus} is not a vague link — it is the place where the threads are actually knotted.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item I can't connect the printer to the computer
  \item I can't get connected
  \item what nectere means
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To connect? (\textbf{Conectar}.) The noun? (\textbf{La conexión} — with an x.) What does \emph{nectere} mean? (\textbf{To tie}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la llamada]{la llamada — the call}

\label{lesson:ES-C469-llamada}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{el pedido} and \textbf{conectar}. One is a thing made from a verb; the other is what you do before the thing will work.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el pedido — the lesson whose table already showed you today's word.
  \item perder — you will want its participle in a moment.
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la llamada}
\textbf{la llamada} — the call.

You have seen this word once, in the middle of somebody else's lesson. \emph{El pedido} listed it as an example of a participle hardened into a noun, and then moved on. Here it is as yours.

\begin{quote}
Voy a hacer una \textbf{llamada}.
\end{quote}

\emph{Devolver la llamada} — to return the call. \emph{Una llamada perdida} — a missed call, the notice your phone leaves you.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the vowel is a rule, the gender is not}]
Which vowel the participle takes is decided for you, and the participle lesson gave you that rule.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{the verb ends} & \textbf{the participle takes} \\
\midrule
\textbf{-ar} & -ado, -ada \\
\textbf{-er}, \textbf{-ir} & -ido, -ida \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{Llamar} is an \emph{-ar} verb, so \emph{-ada}. \emph{Pedir} is an \emph{-ir} verb, so \emph{-ido}. That much you can work out.

What you cannot work out is the \textbf{article}. \emph{El pedido} is masculine. \emph{La llamada} and \emph{la entrada} are feminine. Nothing in \emph{pedir}, \emph{llamar} or \emph{entrar} predicts which way each one went — the gender was settled by whatever noun the participle used to lean on, and that noun is long gone.

So learn the article with the word, the way you learned \emph{el impreso} and \emph{la impresora}. Working out the ending is free; the gender is not.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{Llamada} is \emph{llamar} made into a thing, and \emph{llamar} you have had since the very beginning — the lesson where you learned to say your name traced it to Latin \textbf{clamare}, to cry out, and showed you the \emph{cl-} that became \emph{ll-}.

What is worth adding is how literal the noun still is. A \emph{llamada} is a \textbf{crying-out}, and Spanish has not forgotten it: \emph{una llamada de atención} is a warning — a call for attention, not a phone call at all. The telephone borrowed a word that was already doing the job.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item I am going to make a call
  \item I have to return the call
  \item a missed call
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The call? (\textbf{La llamada}.) From which verb? (\textbf{Llamar}.) Why \emph{-ada} and not \emph{-ida}? (\textbf{Because \emph{llamar} is an -ar verb}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(imprimir, la impresora, conectar, la …]{(imprimir, la impresora, conectar, la llamada) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ES-R469-repaso-oficina}



\begin{quote}
Four words, no prompts. What the machine does, what the machine is, what you do to the machine first, and what you make when it will not work.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: the four, cold}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{English} & \textbf{Spanish} \\
\midrule
to print & \textbf{imprimir} \\
the printer & \textbf{la impresora} \\
to connect & \textbf{conectar} \\
the call & \textbf{la llamada} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: two of these you could have guessed}]
Two of the four were reachable before you were told, and for the same reason: you already held the verb and the ending.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{built from} & \textbf{gives you} \\
\midrule
\emph{imprimir} + \textbf{-dora} & la impresora \\
\emph{llamar} + \textbf{-ada} & la llamada \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{La lavadora} taught the first ending and \emph{el pedido} the second, and \emph{el contador} already warned you that the ending settles nothing about the article. What this chapter added is a case where the article is not only unpredictable but \textbf{meaningful}: \emph{la impresora} is the machine, \emph{el impresor} is the person, and the one letter is the whole difference.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
This chapter put three different routes side by side, and the words look alike on the page whichever route they took.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{how it got here} \\
\midrule
imprimir & inherited — Latin \emph{imprimere}, all the way down \\
conectar & borrowed from English, its parts Latin \\
la llamada & inherited — Latin \emph{clamare}, through \emph{llamar} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{Conectar} is the odd one. It is the only word here whose Latin arrived by way of English, which is why it looks as native as the other three and is not.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item I can't connect the printer, I am going to make a call
  \item which of the four came in through English
  \item the machine and the person, in that order
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To print? (\textbf{Imprimir}.) The printer? (\textbf{La impresora}.) To connect? (\textbf{Conectar}.) The call? (\textbf{La llamada}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{(el aviso de la impresora) — read it, then say what you will do}

\label{lesson:ES-C469-sintesis-oficina}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{la impresora} and \textbf{imprimir}. The notice below is about the first and stops you doing the second.
\end{quote}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,skin=enhanced,colback=orange!6,colframe=orange!45!black,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=1mm,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=4pt,bottom=4pt,fonttitle=\bfseries,title={Read this}]
Taped to the machine:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{AVISO}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
La \textbf{impresora} de la sala 2 está \textbf{fuera de servicio}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
La de la tercera planta \textbf{funciona}.
\end{quote}

And a message from a colleague:

\begin{quote}
No me puedo \textbf{conectar} a internet desde mi ordenador. ¿Puedes \textbf{imprimir} tú el documento? Si no, te \textbf{devuelvo} la \textbf{llamada} en diez minutos.
\end{quote}
\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: what each text asks of you}]
The notice reports a state. The message asks for something and offers a way out if the answer is no. They want different replies.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{the notice} & \textbf{the message} \\
\midrule
\emph{está fuera de servicio} & \emph{¿puedes imprimir tú el documento?} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Two details in the message repay a second look.

\textbf{La de la tercera planta.} The notice drops \emph{impresora} and leaves \emph{la} standing for it. Spanish does this freely once the noun is on the table, and a notice will do it to save a line.

\textbf{¿Puedes imprimir tú?} The \emph{tú} is not needed for the grammar — the verb already says who. It is there to point: \emph{you}, rather than me, because I cannot. A pronoun that could be dropped and is not is doing work.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say which printer is broken and which one works, using \emph{la} on its own for the second the way the notice does.

Now answer the message: say you will print the document, and say why your colleague could not — the connection, not the machine.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is wrong with the machine? (\textbf{Está fuera de servicio}.) What is wrong for your colleague? (\textbf{No se puede conectar}.) What will you do? (\textbf{Imprimir el documento}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
